newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: FOCUS-Nestle sees profit rising in 1996.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Nestle sees profit rising in 1996.

text.p: Nestle SA on Wednesday said it was optimistic for 1996, forecasting that group net profit would surpass three billion Swiss francs ($2.4 billion), thanks in part to favourable currency exchange rates.
The world's biggest food company said that for the first time in a few years, exchange rates had a beneficial impact on Nestle's results.
The Swiss franc's recent declines have been positive for export-dependent firms based in Switzerland.

"Unless there is a very volatile turn-around in the currency market, we can expect net profits to grow faster than sales. In absolute terms they will certainly exceed three billion (francs)," Nestle chairman Helmut Maucher told journalists gathered at the company's headquarters for presentation of its 10-month results.
"We are expecting to finish the year with turnover of close to 60 billion ($47.4 billion) unless unexpectedly volatile currency fluctuations take place in the meantime," he said.

His forecast compared with consolidated net profits in 1995 of 2.92 billion francs ($2.3 billion), and sales of 56.48 billion ($44.6 billion). Maucher declined to be drawn on whether Nestle could match 1994's record profit of 3.25 billion, which included extraordinary gains.
Maucher said he was optimistic about growth continuing in the coming years, but provided no figures.
"I am an optimist as to continued growth in trade and net consolidated profit for next year as well as for the years to come," Maucher said.

He refused to rule out a higher dividend on 1996 results, noting the payout would increase if profits rose and the company's board maintained its current policy of distributing about a third of profits to shareholders, but said a decision was still pending.

Maucher also said the company was not seeking big acquisitions at present because prices were relatively high and the company faced anti-cartel laws. But if the right opportunity emerged "then our policy would change in a second".

Nestle said its sales for the first 10 months of 1996 grew 5.7 percent versus the comparable 1995 period, to 48.3 billion Swiss francs ($38.1 billion) from 45.7 billion ($36.1 billion) in the 1995 10 months.

Sales volume growth in January to October was three percent, a slight slowing from the 3.6 percent reported for the first half as inclement weather in Europe hurt sales of ice cream and mineral water.
Beverage sales rose only 1.1 percent in Swiss franc terms because of bad weather and lower coffee prices that masked good volume growth in the United States, finance chief Mario Corti said.
Sales of ready-made meals and kitchen products were up 7.4 percent, chocolate and confectionery turnover rose 7.1 percent, and pharmaceutical products were up 12.6 percent.

Sales appeared to be turning higher in the second half of 1996, with October turnover up 12 percent versus October 1995. But he said sales so far have not developed in a "completely satisfying" manner.
But he said sales were moving ahead briskly in Eastern Europe, up some 50 percent, and in Asia, showing double-digit growth.
